arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts asked what relief Olivier would get from other burdens of his conviction, such as a firearms restriction, and whether those burdens would block the lawsuit.
Justice Jackson asked whether a probationary condition tied to his prior sentence would be eliminated if he won the lawsuit.
Justice Gorsuch pressed a lawyer to pursue a hypothetical further, saying the lawyer was fighting the hypothetical rather than engaging with it.

case.dek: Gabriel Olivier was arrested for preaching in a Brandon, Mississippi park and convicted under a city ordinance. He now asks the Supreme Court whether he can sue under federal civil rights law to block future prosecutions under that ordinance, even though his conviction stands.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Olivier says his Christian faith calls him to preach in city parks. He argues the ordinance criminalizes his religious speech and that federal civil rights law lets him seek prospective relief against future enforcement.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A lower court ruled against Olivier. He asked the Supreme Court to reverse that decision and let his lawsuit proceed. The city asked the Supreme Court to affirm the lower court and dismiss the case.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Olivier wants permission to sue under federal civil rights law for prospective relief protecting him from future prosecution under the ordinance.
The city wants the Supreme Court to affirm the lower court, saying Olivier had chances to challenge the ordinance during his prosecution and appeals.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Olivier's lawyer argued the ordinance criminalizes his religious speech and that a prior conviction does not bar prospective relief under federal civil rights law.
The city's lawyer argued Olivier had the opportunity to challenge the ordinance's constitutionality in the Mississippi trial court, on direct appeal, and by petitioning the Supreme Court.
